The educational sector has seen a significant rise in multimodal content development, 
which necessitates the use of advanced machine learning techniques to analyze 
complex multimedia such as videos, infographics, and interactive simulations. 
However, current models are limited by their inability to effectively process 
multimodal information, resulting in subpar performance across various educational 
fields. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that integrates 
multimodal fusion with knowledge distillation to enhance the generalizability 
of educational models. Specifically, we utilize a multimodal fusion module 
to merge diverse modalities and a knowledge distillation module to transfer 
expertise from a pre-trained teacher model to a student model. Experimental 
results on multiple educational datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, 
yielding superior performance compared to existing methods. The code and datasets 
can be accessed at https://github.com/zhengda1234567/MultimodalKnowledgeDistillation.

under Grant No. 52106223. The corresponding author is zhangda1234567@163.com.

to the advancement of the educational AI community. Ultimately, we hope this 
research can facilitate the development of more effective educational AI systems.

innovation in this area.

Off-policy evaluation in reinforcement learning seeks to estimate the expected outcome of a given policy using data from a behavior policy. This field has seen significant advancements, yet the convergence rates of many leading estimators remain unclear. This paper examines the convergence rates of various estimators under different conditions, including the realizability assumption, and finds that they exhibit polynomial or exponential convergence. We also identify the limitations of these estimators and propose a new approach that achieves faster convergence without relying on the realizability assumption. This new estimator is shown to converge at a rate comparable to online learning methods and outperforms existing ones in off-policy evaluation tasks. Our research demonstrates the potential of a new family of estimators that can be applied to a broader range of problems, including those in off-policy evaluation and online learning. We also provide a theoretical framework for understanding the convergence rates of these estimators and highlight their connection to the concept of "statistical regret." By leveraging this adaptive framework, we successfully optimize gate sequences for the generation of complex quantum states using only basic two-qubit gates and their conjugates. Notably, this method allows for the efficient creation of high-fidelity states with high fidelity and reduced gate count compared to existing algorithms. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the exploration of a vast solution space to identify the most suitable gate sequence for a given quantum state. To illustrate the capabilities of this adaptive method, we demonstrate its application in generating complex quantum states and their associated gate sequences using the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm. As a result, we obtain gate sequences that achieve high fidelity and fidelity, and significantly reduce the time required for state preparation. Ultimately, this adaptive framework empowers users to identify the most effective gate sequence for a given quantum state without requiring extensive problem formulation expertise. Furthermore, our ablation studies reveal that the heterogeneous representation ensemble is a key factor contributing to its superior performance. The findings of this study highlight the potential of the heterogeneous representation ensemble in fake news classification and offer valuable insights for future research in this area. This paper presents a novel CNN approach for enhancing the visual quality of
images obtained from low-light RAW data, a task typically associated with noise
reduction. Building upon the observation that camera sensors are designed to
minimize noise while maintaining image details, we propose a two-stage deep
learning strategy that first estimates noise from RAW data and then applies a
noise reduction technique. We utilize a CNN to predict noise levels, leveraging
the fact that noisy pixels tend to have higher values, and another CNN to
generate denoised images. We also introduce a noise estimation loss function
based on the relationship between estimated noise and low-level image features.
Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in image
enhancement, outperforming existing methods in both subjective and objective
evaluations. The code and models can be accessed at https://github.com/kecsen/RAWNoise.

The graph of the Weierstrass sigma function $\sigma(z)$ of a rational function of genus g defines a curve of genus 1, with algebraic invariants $g_2$ and $g_3$, which can be expressed as polynomials in the coefficients of the initial function. This note demonstrates that these invariants are optimal limits for specific polynomial expressions formed from the coefficients of the function. Furthermore, it is shown that such curves of genus 1 can be characterized by their coefficient relationships, which are a subset of all possible combinations. Finally, it is established that such a curve exists with a specific set of invariants by constructing one explicitly. This research was motivated by an inquiry from David Bourqui regarding the optimal limits for such a curve's invariants, to which the answer proved to be more complex than initially anticipated. Ultimately, it is found that these optimal limits are not the sole values for which such a curve exists, with additional values depending on the specific set of invariants in question. Our study also examines functional connectivity data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and shows that site-specific effects can significantly impact the accuracy of network-based analyses, highlighting the importance of considering these effects in neuroimaging studies. The proposed method is widely applicable to various neuroimaging studies, including those examining resting-state fMRI data. This metric assesses the resilience of convolutional neural networks by comparing the accuracy of their predictions when faced with distorted images to their accuracy when faced with undisturbed images.  Through a series of experiments conducted on the CIFAR-10 dataset, we have found that the Robustness Ratio is a more effective indicator of a model's ability to withstand input disruptions than traditional evaluation methods.  Furthermore, we have discovered that the robustness of these models can be significantly enhanced by incorporating techniques such as adversarial training and data augmentation.  Our research findings are expected to contribute to a better understanding of the robustness of deep neural networks and to serve as a valuable resource for researchers working in this area. This study presents a groundbreaking method for identifying and measuring cache side-channel vulnerabilities within real-world software.  The proposed approach is the first to offer a comprehensive solution for detecting such vulnerabilities in production environments.  By leveraging a combination of static source code analysis and dynamic execution, our method enables the detection and quantification of side-channel risks.  The static phase pinpoints potential vulnerability sources, while the dynamic phase determines the sensitivity of victim code and identifies attacks.  The method also allows for the calculation of attack intensity, providing a comprehensive understanding of side-channel risks. The phenomenon of mode collapse in generative models, where the distribution of generated images is concentrated around a limited number of underlying classes, has been extensively documented. Despite numerous proposed solutions, the issue persists in various forms across different models, hindering their practical applications. In this research, we investigate mode collapse as a problem of high-dimensional density estimation and propose a novel approach that leverages the Hessian matrix to identify and mitigate this problem. By analyzing the Hessian eigenvalues, we demonstrate that they can serve as a reliable indicator for mode collapse. Furthermore, we develop a regularization strategy that utilizes Hessian eigenvalues to prevent mode collapse. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to a broad range of generative models, including VAEs, GANs, and other variants. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in maintaining a diverse range of classes in the latent space, as measured by the Hessian eigenvalues. Additionally, we show that our method can be used to improve the performance of pre-trained models, as the Hessian eigenvalues provide a more accurate assessment of mode collapse than the latent space metrics. In the context of geometrically ergodic state transition models, we examine the properties of decentralized estimators in a two-actor setup, where each actor has access to incomplete information and can only observe a subset of the available data. Our analysis reveals that, as the number of actors increases, the discrepancy between the decentralized estimate and the central estimate converges to zero at a rate comparable to the central estimate's own precision. This understanding has practical implications, particularly in the design of decentralized systems seeking to replicate the effectiveness of their central counterpart. Notably, our findings are demonstrated through applications in hidden Markov models and stochastic processes with Markov dependencies. The results are also extended to accommodate the case of a large number of actors, where the data is distributed across multiple servers, and the calculation of the central estimate becomes computationally infeasible. In this scenario, we establish that, as the number of actors increases, the discrepancy between the decentralized estimate and the central estimate diminishes at a rate proportional to the inverse of the square root of the number of actors. Our analysis is further supported by the presentation of numerical examples. Ultimately, we also explore the potential for distributed data analysis in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. Centralized radio access networks (C-RANs) are hindered by limited fronthaul capacity, which necessitates the development of efficient resource management techniques. A new distributed C-RAN architecture, which utilizes edge caching, has been proposed to address this challenge. By integrating caching and distributed processing, this framework enables base stations to efficiently process data locally, thereby reducing data transmission over the limited fronthaul link. However, this framework's performance is influenced by the cache placement strategy, which is a complex optimization problem. To address this challenge, we formulate a joint caching and beamforming optimization problem for downlink transmissions in this distributed C-RAN, which involves minimizing maximum achievable rate subject to cache constraints. We develop a novel algorithm to solve this optimization problem, which leverages the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) to derive a closed-form solution. Simulation results demonstrate that this algorithm significantly outperforms conventional C-RANs in terms of average rate sum capacity and peak rate sum capacity. Furthermore, it is shown that this algorithm can achieve optimal performance asymptotically. Additionally, we evaluate the impact of imperfect channel state information on the proposed scheme, which is found to be robust to channel estimation errors. to any message. The security of Wink has been formally analyzed using a

Our innovative approach to secret image hiding, SABMIS, employs a unique
combination of sparse approximation-based matching pursuit and binary
morphological ranking evolution. This method successfully embeds multiple secret
images within a single cover image by utilizing an optimized hidden-Seek algorithm.
SABMIS's embedding capacity is significantly higher for one, two, three, and four
hidden images compared to existing techniques like SABMIS1 and SABMIS2. This
technique's robustness is further demonstrated by its ability to withstand common
attacks like the double threshold attack, median cut attack, and amplitude scaling attack.
Extensive experiments confirm the superior performance of SABMIS over other
state-of-the-art methods in terms of both quality and security. Moreover, our
method's high security is also verified through a security analysis based on the
two-dimensional cross correlation function. This technique's flexibility is also
demonstrated by its ability to accommodate various cover image types, including
grayscale and binary images. Additionally, our method's ability to hide multiple
images within a single cover image is further enhanced by its ability to embed up to four
secret images within a single cover image. This makes SABMIS a highly efficient and secure technique.

We investigate the vertex cover problem, where the goal is to select a minimum number of vertices to cover all other vertices in a given graph. Our focus is on bipartite graphs, for which we develop an algorithm that achieves a performance ratio of $\frac{2(f-1)}{f}$, given that a subset of vertices $S$ has a factor ratio of $f$ compared to the optimal solution. Our method involves constructing a specific graph, solving a related problem on it, and utilizing its properties to derive a feasible solution for the original vertex cover problem. Our results demonstrate that including an arbitrary set of vertices can significantly improve the performance ratio, as it can be as high as 2 for sufficiently large factor ratios. This is in contrast to the scenario where no such vertices are present, for which the best known performance ratio is 2, achieved by Berman and Kozlovski. Our algorithm also yields a polynomial time solution, with a runtime of $O(m^3 \log m)$, where $m$ denotes the number of edges in the graph. Furthermore, we establish that our method can be adapted to obtain a randomized solution with an expected performance ratio of $\frac{2(f-1)}{f}$, provided that the graph is a bipartite random graph. Our algorithm can be further modified to obtain a deterministic solution with an improved performance ratio of $\frac{2\sqrt{f-1}}{\sqrt{f}}$, for sufficiently large factor ratios. Our results also extend to the edge cover problem, for which we develop an algorithm that achieves a performance ratio of $\frac{2(f-1)}{f}$, given that a subset of edges $S$ has a factor ratio of $f$ compared to the optimal solution. Our method involves constructing a specific graph, solving a related problem on it, and utilizing its properties to derive a feasible solution for the edge cover problem. Our results demonstrate that including an arbitrary set of edges can be beneficial, as it can be as high as $\frac{2\sqrt{1.5f}}{\sqrt{f}}$ for sufficiently large factor ratios. This is in contrast to the scenario where no such edges are present, for which the best known performance ratio is 2, achieved by König. Our algorithm can be adapted to obtain a randomized solution with an expected performance ratio of $\frac{2\sqrt{1.5f}}{\sqrt{f}}$, provided that the graph is a bipartite random graph.

We introduce FOON, a task tree formalism that enables the automated generation of recipes from user-specified ingredients and cooking methods. FOON recipes are generated through a planning process that breaks down complex tasks into simpler subtasks, which are then executed in a step-by-step fashion. Utilizing the planning framework, we developed a recipe generator called FOON-Recipe, which leverages user-defined task trees to produce recipes tailored to specific taste preferences. To evaluate the efficacy of FOON-Recipe, we compared its performance with human-generated recipes in terms of correctness, completeness, and novelty. The results indicate that FOON-Recipe outperforms its human counterparts in all three areas, producing safer, more comprehensive, and innovative recipes. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that FOON recipes can be optimized through the strategic selection of task variables, such as action parameters and ingredient quantities. To facilitate the wider adoption of FOON, we have created a web-based tool that allows users to define custom cooking trees and generate recipes from them. This research contributes to the development of a novel approach to recipe planning, offering a promising solution for the creation of personalized recipes. Location-based services rely on user location data, but sharing this information poses significant privacy risks.  To address these concerns, companies often have the option to provide users with location data encryption.  However, existing encryption methods compromise user privacy by requiring precise location calculations or introducing significant computational overhead.  To mitigate these drawbacks, we developed a new system that encrypts user location data in real-time, using approximate calculations that provide users with more control over their private information.  Our solution involves a two-layered approach: the first layer allows users to adjust the trade-off between location accuracy and privacy, while the second layer uses machine learning to suggest locations based on user preferences.  Our experiments demonstrate that this approach can significantly reduce computational costs, achieving a 3.5-fold increase in speed compared to existing methods.  Moreover, our system can process up to 1,000 location updates per second, making it suitable for real-world applications.  Our findings also highlight the importance of user involvement in setting personal privacy boundaries, underscoring the need for user control over their personal data.  To our knowledge, this study is the first to explore the dynamic trade-off between location accuracy and privacy, and to provide users with the ability to manage their own privacy levels. Theoretical results show that this method provides strong control over the FDR in dependent data, with simulation results demonstrating its superiority to existing methods. The method is further illustrated through an application to real-world data analysis. In software development, feature toggles are widely used to enable teams to work in an agile manner by allowing them to quickly deploy incomplete features for testing purposes. Our study investigates the impact of feature toggles on the development process by analyzing data from 27 open-source projects. Our results show that the use of feature toggles leads to a significant decrease in the number of code branch merges, which in turn results in fewer conflicts being resolved. Furthermore, we found that the deployment of features using toggles takes longer compared to traditional deployment methods, indicating that teams are likely testing features for a longer period before releasing them. Additionally, we found that the majority of features using togges are eventually removed, and this process tends to occur earlier than the typical time frame for such changes. These findings suggest that teams may benefit from adopting feature togges, as they can help teams work more efficiently by reducing the time spent on code branch merges and deploying features. However, further research is needed to determine whether these benefits translate to production environments. Our study's findings can serve as a guide for teams considering the adoption of feature togges, and provide insights for future research on their use in software development. We introduce a novel self-supervised approach to denoising, which employs a single model to remove noise from various types of data. This method, known as AutoDenoise, utilizes a denoising autoencoder that is trained using a diverse set of noisy data from different domains. AutoDenoise is a straightforward yet effective technique that enables the model to generalize across various data types. We evaluated AutoDenoise on a range of image, audio, and text denoising tasks and found that it outperforms or matches the performance of specialized models in each domain. Additionally, our results demonstrate that AutoDenoise's generalization capabilities extend across different data types, enabling it to achieve comparable performance to domain-specific models. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel framework called You Only Hear Once (YOHO), which employs a sliding window to classify audio segments. Diabetic foot ulcers pose a significant health risk to diabetic patients, necessitating regular monitoring to prevent severe complications.  Current monitoring methods rely on manual evaluation of wound images, which can be time-consuming and may lead to suboptimal treatment decisions due to subjective interpretation.  To address this challenge, we propose an innovative approach that utilizes image-to-image translation to create a database of standardized, annotated wound images.  Specifically, we employ a style transfer technique to generate realistic images of diabetic foot ulcers based on patient medical histories, then leverage an image-to-image translation model to predict the optimal treatment outcomes.  To validate our approach, we compiled a dataset of 1,500 images from the University of Texas Medical Branch's wound care clinic, and evaluated the performance of our models using metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and visual inspection.  Our results demonstrate that the generated images are highly realistic and the optimal treatment outputs are accurate, indicating that this method has the potential to support the development of an intelligent decision support system for diabetic foot ulcer monitoring. This research applies the principles of optimal transport to develop a framework for assessing fairness in machine learning models. The approach views fairness as a trade-off between group performance and group membership-based discrimination, and it quantifies fairness as the optimal transport cost between relevant population groups. By using the geometry of optimal transport, the framework can be extended to cover various fairness criteria, including equality of opportunity and equalized odds, and it provides a way to test for significant disparities in these criteria through statistical analysis. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through a series of simulations and real-world applications in predicting student performance and loan default risk. The results show that the optimal transport framework offers a more nuanced understanding of group performance differences and data-driven insights into the limitations of current fairness criteria in machine learning. The approach also highlights the importance of considering the underlying data-generating processes when evaluating fairness in machine learning models. Recent breakthroughs in real-time semantic segmentation have been achieved by innovative approaches that utilize cross-resolution attention. These methods leverage the distinct spatial details of features from multiple scales to enhance segmentation performance. However, existing cross-resolution attention techniques often overlook the inherent hierarchical structure of multi-scale features, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel cross-resolution attention module, called the Cross-attention Hierarchical Fusion (CHF) module, which effectively leverages the complementary information between features from different scales. By incorporating a hierarchical fusion mechanism, CHF enables the efficient aggregation of information across multiple scales, resulting in a more robust and accurate segmentation model. Extensive experiments on widely-used benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach, which achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods while significantly reducing computational complexity. A novel layer selection algorithm then leverages this graph to strategically prune network layers, reducing the computational cost of models. Our research focuses on developing a robust 3D object detection system that can efficiently process point cloud data by leveraging neural networks. addressing privacy concerns.  However, the pursuit of fairness in FL remains an unsolved issue, 
as each client's interests are often compromised by the aggregation of contributions.  This study

by producing unique, localized models.  A novel approach is proposed, utilizing a fairness-aware 
quantization method that minimizes the differences between centralized and decentralized models. 
This framework's effectiveness is validated through a series of experiments on both synthetic and 
real-world datasets, revealing the benefits of balancing privacy and fairness in FL.  The results show 
that our proposed framework yields fairer models while maintaining reasonable levels of privacy.

This research delves into how political parties utilize voter networks to disseminate information, focusing on their advertising tactics in response to perceived inequalities in information distribution within these networks. We analyze voter networks from the 2014 European Parliament elections in Germany, employing clustering to identify homogenous groups of voters and assessing the impact of party advertising on these clusters. Our findings indicate that parties with limited financial resources target core supporters and key influencers in densely connected voter clusters, while wealthier parties broadly promote their brand across various voter communities. We also examine how information dynamics influence electoral outcomes and reveal that voters in densely connected groups tend to adopt similar opinions, leading to a more predictable voting behavior. Ultimately, our study highlights the strategic value of voter networks for political parties seeking to effectively disseminate information and shape public opinion. The developed methodology can be applied to other social phenomena and is not confined to the context of political advertising. Furthermore, this research underscores the importance of studying voter networks in electoral competition, providing valuable insights for political marketing and campaign strategy. The asymmetry difference between $D^0$ and $\overline{D}^0$ is a crucial indicator of CP-violation in the charm sector. The difference in CP-violating asymmetries, denoted as $A_{CP}$, is measured in the $K^0_S\pi^+\pi^-$ decay channel from 1.9 fb$^{-1}$ of $\sqrt{s}=1.96$ TeV proton-antiproton collision data obtained using the D0 detector. The analysis yields a CP-violation difference of 0.0024 $\pm$ 0.0024 (statistical) $\pm$ 0.0011 (systematic), with a total uncertainty of 0.0035. This measurement is the first to reach the precision of 1% and aligns with the standard model prediction of zero CP-violation. Furthermore, the individual asymmetries of $A_{CP}(K^0_S\pi^+)$ and $A_{CP}(K^0_S\pi^-)$ are also determined. The combined results of $A_{CP}(K^0_S\pi^+)$ and $A_{CP}(K^0_S\pi^-)$ yield a CP-violation difference of 0.0023 $\pm$ 0.0021 (statistical) $\pm$ 0.0011 (systematic), consistent with the total CP-violation difference of 0.0024. These findings provide new insights into CP-violation in the charm sector. The first observation of $D^0$ decays to $K^0_S\pi^+\pi^-$ is also reported. The branching ratio for this decay is estimated to be (2.8 $\pm$ 0.9 $\pm$ 0.2) $\times 10^{-5}$. The measurement of $A_{CP}$ is also compared with the predictions of various models, such as the factorization model and the QCD long-distance model. In the context of federated learning, a collaborative approach among multiple clients, we introduce a novel method called pFedHN. This approach enables the simultaneous training of multiple personalized models with reduced communication costs. By leveraging a shared space of models and a set of carefully designed updates, pFedHN efficiently trains a distinct model for each user. Notably, our method requires the same number of communications as training a single personal model with a FedAvg-based method. Experimental results demonstrate that pFedHN outperforms the FedAvg-based approach, even when the number of communications is limited. Additionally, our method exhibits improved efficiency and accuracy when compared to other state-of-the-art methods that require fewer communications. Recommender systems have been enhanced by the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in recent years.  However, existing GNN-based methods for recommendations have several limitations.  They often rely on pre-defined node attributes, which can be insufficient for capturing complex user-item relationships.  Furthermore, these methods often overlook the impact of user and item attributes on the recommendation process.  To address these issues, we propose a novel GNN-based recommendation system called BC-GCN, which incorporates both graph and attribute-based information.  By utilizing the BC Loss function, we can effectively incorporate attribute information into the GNN's message passing mechanism, which can be used to compute both graph and attribute-based representations.  Experimental results on several datasets demonstrate that BC-GCN outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, with improvements of up to 9.5% in terms of Recall and 4.1% in terms of NDCG.  Additionally, we found that BC-GCN can be effectively combined with other GNN-based methods to further enhance their performance. Recent advancements in pose transfer algorithms have garnered significant interest, 
enabling the transfer of a person's pose from one image to another image. 
However, existing algorithms often fail to produce realistic results in real-world applications. 
This limitation arises from the fact that these algorithms rely on a fixed set of parameters, 
which are often insufficient to capture the complexity of human poses. 
To address this issue, we propose a novel pose transfer approach that incorporates 
a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) and a variational encoder-decoder (VED). 
The VED is specifically designed to handle challenging pose transfer tasks, 
enabling the generation of more realistic and diverse results. 
To further enhance the approach, we incorporate a novel loss function that promotes 
realism and diversity in the generated images. 
Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing pose transfer methods, 
yielding more realistic and diverse results in the process. 
The proposed method is also shown to be effective in the context of a pose transfer challenge, 
where it successfully handles difficult scenarios involving complex poses.

We introduce PMD-PD, a novel policy gradient algorithm, specifically designed to optimize the policy in constrained Markov decision processes. This algorithm incorporates both the policy gradient and natural policy gradient, updating the policy with a combination of step and trust region adjustments. We establish that PMD-PD converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{N})$ and simultaneously ensures that the constrained policy remains invariant. We demonstrate that PMD-PD outperforms existing methods in terms of both theoretical convergence and practical application, as evidenced by its implementation in the Markov chain controller. Additionally, we showcase the algorithm's effectiveness through its successful optimization of the policy in constrained deep reinforcement learning models. This work bridges the gap between theoretical and practical optimization of constrained Markov decision processes, while also introducing a new approach to constrained policy gradient methods. Furthermore, this method can be trained without relying on ground truth data, utilizing a loss function that minimizes the difference between consecutive frames' features. The M copula serves as a statistical model for capturing various forms of mixed dependencies among random variables, where the subscript 'M' symbolizes the complexity of interactions between the variables, which can range from minimal (e.g., two variables) to extensive. In cases where the variables exhibit intricate, high-order dependencies, the M copula emerges as a vital tool for analysis. This document outlines the foundational aspects of the M copula, along with its applications in the fields of engineering, finance, and medicine. Additionally, it presents a novel method for identifying the order of dependence within the M copula, which is based on the application of the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion to the partial autocorrelation function derived from the copula parameters. The proposed approach is demonstrated through a combination of simulated data sets and real-world examples from engineering, finance, and medicine, which showcase the efficacy of the method. The findings presented in this document are expected to contribute to the advancement of statistical modeling techniques for analyzing complex systems and networks. A significant challenge in active learning arises when data points lack labels, making it difficult to assess their gradients. This paper tackles this issue by developing two methods to estimate the gradient magnitude of unmarked data points: one based on local data approximation via the k-nearest neighbors, and the other utilizing a neural network to predict the gradient norm. The proposed solutions are integrated into the Probabilistic Margin-based Active Learning (PMAL) framework, which leverages the probabilistic margins of the support vector machine (SVM) to guide active learning. The effectiveness of the modified PMAL is evaluated on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIL datasets, demonstrating the superiority of the neural network estimator over the k-nearest neighbors approach. The results also highlight the advantages of the proposed approaches over random sampling and the Permutation Importance method. In the field of 3D Computer Vision, geometric transformations are a crucial aspect, 
and spatial transformer networks can learn to be invariant to such transformations by 
directly learning the mapping between coordinates. However, existing spatial 
transformer networks are limited by their reliance on fixed grids, which cannot be 
adapted to the needs of the network. In this research, we introduce a dynamic spatial 
transformer network that learns a non-linear coordinate transformation, allowing it 
to be invariant to 3D geometric transformations like rotation and translation. The 
proposed method consists of a network that generates a dynamic grid based on the 
input point cloud, followed by a series of convolutional layers that process the 
dynamic grid. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three tasks: 
point cloud registration, 3D object detection, and point cloud segmentation. The 
results show that our method outperforms existing spatial transformer networks in 
all three tasks, achieving a 1.5% improvement in point cloud registration, a 2.5% 
improvement in 3D object detection, and a 1.5% improvement in point cloud 
segmentation. The code for our method is available on GitHub at the specified link. 
Our research contributes to the field of 3D geometric deep learning and highlights the 
importance of dynamic grids in spatial transformer networks. We also provide a 
comparative analysis of our method with existing spatial transformer networks. 
Finally, we conduct an ablation study to validate the effectiveness of our method.

Machine learning systems are increasingly being held to high safety standards, 
necessitating ongoing monitoring for potential safety threats.  However, identifying 
when a system crosses a threshold from safe to unsafe operation remains a significant 
challenge.  In this study, we investigate the difficulties in monitoring phase 
transitions within machine learning models, which can be due to the intricate nature 
of the transition or the limitations of the available data.  To address this issue, 
we propose a new framework for monitoring phase transitions, which involves 
developing a model to forecast the likelihood of a transition occurring.  We test 
this approach on a range of simulated and real-world datasets, which include image 
recognition and autonomous driving tasks.  Our results indicate that this framework 
can be an effective tool for machine learning practitioners to monitor potential 
phase transitions and thus ensure the ongoing safety of their systems.  Furthermore, 
we discuss the broader implications of our findings for machine learning security.

The Visual Question Answering task, where a model generates answers to questions based on images, has seen significant advancements in recent years.  However, existing VQA models are limited by their inability to generalize to real-world applications, where the image and question distributions do not align. The performance of pre-trained video models heavily relies on the video clip selection and sampling strategy used. However, existing approaches often involve a time-consuming process of random sampling and subsequent fine-tuning, which can be impractical. This paper proposes a novel tuning paradigm for video classification that enables the direct optimization of the video sampling distribution, thereby eliminating the need for fine-tuning. By leveraging a faster-than-exponential convergence guarantee, the method accelerates the training process by an order of magnitude compared to random sampling. Additionally, the proposed approach can adapt to different network architectures and can even be applied to other types of pre-trained models. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, which achieves comparable or better performance than state-of-the-art methods while reducing the training time from multiple hours to minutes. In aerial guidance applications, the effectiveness of a guidance system can be significantly enhanced by incorporating information about the state of the human operator, rather than solely relying on the state of the robot.
This paper presents a novel controller that utilizes human-state information to improve aerial guidance, which is based on a model predictive control (MPC) strategy that takes into account the dynamics of both the robot and the human.
The proposed MPC controller is designed to minimize the time required for the robot to reach the target while ensuring the safety of both the robot and the human, and it is compared to a conventional MPC controller that only considers the robot's state. The results demonstrate that the proposed controller significantly outperforms the conventional controller in terms of speed and human safety. Additionally, the benefits of the proposed controller are validated through simulations of a human-robot interaction scenario. The accompanying video presents a real-world demonstration of the proposed controller in action. The complete design and implementation details of the proposed controller are provided for the sake of reproducibility. A new method for forecasting mortality rates has been developed, taking into account the dynamic nature of factor loadings associated with various demographic groups. This approach is based on a factor model that considers the distribution of life expectancy to be influenced by multiple underlying risk factors. Estimating the factor loadings and making predictions about future mortality rates are interconnected tasks, which can be effectively addressed through a joint estimation and forecasting framework. By combining the factor loadings with a specific risk factor, the proposed model provides accurate 10-year forecasts of mortality rates for different demographic groups. Experimental results demonstrate that this model outperforms traditional methods, particularly when dealing with groups of intermediate size, by leveraging the information from related subgroups. Furthermore, the proposed model's ability to forecast mortality rates for specific age groups is significantly improved when compared to the traditional Lee-Carter method. Additionally, the model's performance is evaluated using alternative risk factors, such as those derived from the Galton-Crammer model, and the results indicate that the proposed approach is more accurate than the traditional Galton-Crammer model. All the necessary code to replicate these findings is made available online. Estimating heart rate from video recordings is a complex task, especially when the video is of poor quality. Current methods often struggle to accurately track heart rate in such scenarios. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach called IBIS-CNN, which leverages a unique combination of image processing and signal analysis. By first enhancing the video, then extracting relevant features, and finally using a machine learning model to track heart rate, IBIS-CNN significantly outperforms existing methods on low-quality video. In fact, IBIS-CNN achieved an impressive increase of 9.1% in accuracy over the previous best result on a widely used benchmark dataset. Moreover, IBIS-CNN's ability to accurately track heart rate in low-light conditions was also demonstrated, outscoring the top-performing method by a margin of 5.1%. This paper introduces a novel network architecture that leverages a centralized controller to manage data flows efficiently. By integrating local switches and remote nodes, the proposed network enables the centralized controller to optimize data flows. We demonstrate that the centralized controller can mitigate data burstiness by strategically utilizing local buffers and remote nodes, with the length of local buffers being inversely proportional to the burstiness of data streams. We also establish that the proposed network's throughput is directly determined by the centralized controller's decision regarding the length of local buffers. Furthermore, we present a practical implementation of the centralized controller, based on the Proportional Integral Derivative algorithm, to manage local buffer lengths and data flows effectively. We validate the proposed network architecture through simulations, comparing its performance with that of traditional networks lacking centralized control, and show that it can achieve higher throughput and reduce data burstiness effectively. Ultimately, our results highlight the benefits of centralized control in managing data flows and burstiness in networks. The presented work is part of a broader research effort to develop a comprehensive network architecture for the Internet of Things. Recent advancements in Learned Indexing research have shown that machine-learned data structures can outperform traditional ones. This paper introduces a novel neural network design tailored for Learned Indexes, which significantly reduces their memory consumption and training complexity. Our proposed network leverages the benefits of being sparse, thereby eliminating the need for a vast number of parameters, and incorporates a novel training method that enables the network to learn optimal parameter configurations. This design is complemented by a new inference technique that capitalizes on the network's sparsity. A novel, low-rank based optimization technique has been proposed for efficiently solving the problem of optimal transport (OT) between two datasets, which involves a trade-off between minimizing the cost of transportation and promoting sparsity. Diverging from conventional approaches, this method does not rely on the regularization of entropy. Instead, it incorporates a low-rank constraint on the OT matrix, which is directly parameterized. The proposed method has been shown to be computationally efficient, achieving a runtime complexity of O(n^3), whereas conventional approaches typically have a runtime complexity of O(n^4). The effectiveness of the proposed method has been demonstrated through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. The accompanying code can be found on the following repository: https://github.com/kehanma/lowrank-ot. A web-based demo is also available at https://opt-transport.github.io. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) have garnered significant attention in the field of deep learning due to their potential to mimic the brain's functionality. However, SNNs still face a significant hurdle in achieving accuracy comparable to traditional deep learning networks. This paper proposes a novel training method for SNNs that incorporates a two-stage approach. Initially, the network is trained using a spike-triggered backpropagation algorithm, and then the weights are fine-tuned using a stochastic gradient descent mechanism. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by achieving a top-1 accuracy of 62.4% on the CIFAR-10 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art by a substantial margin. Moreover, the proposed approach yields a significant reduction in spike rates, decreasing it by 50% compared to the previous best results. This paper also presents a comprehensive analysis of the network's performance, including its accuracy, spike rates, and cross-correlation matrices. We further investigate the impact of various hyperparameters on the network's performance and provide a detailed comparison with existing training methods. Finally, the proposed approach is successfully applied to the CIFAR-100 dataset, achieving a top-1 accuracy of 53.8% with a competitive performance. We introduce T-BERT, a novel trace retrieval system that leverages pre-trained language models to enhance the accuracy of identifying relationships between scientific documents. T-BERT surpasses traditional information retrieval models by a significant margin of 7.3% in terms of the mean reciprocal rank, and it outperforms a leading open-source system by 2.1%. The proposed T-BERT framework also paves the way for the application of pre-trained language models in other trace retrieval systems. The approach is validated through experiments on satellite images of the Canadian High Arctic, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods in the field. The integration of uncertainty quantification is found to significantly enhance the network's ability to predict the presence of glaciers in challenging cases, such as in areas with complex ice morphology. entity type information into the decoding process. However, existing methods have
their limitations, as they either rely on pre-trained language models or require
additional entity typing tasks. To address this, we introduce a new approach that
learns entity type representations within a neural encoder-decoder model. The
encoder processes input data to generate contextual representations, which are
then used to inform the decoder, and we utilize a novel soft-labeling mechanism
to model entity type distributions. Experimental results on multiple datasets
demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, and further analysis reveals that
our entity type representations are more robust than those generated by other
approaches. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/chenFWh/AIE-T5.

We establish a general framework for functional convexity, which encompasses
various inequalities in convex geometry, and also reveals connections to information
theoretic problems. Specifically, we demonstrate that a volume-based log-submodular
property leads to a refined version of the Brunn-Minkowski inequality. Furthermore,
we show that convex functions related to MCMC sampling satisfy logarithmic submodularity
and, as a result, prove that their expectations exhibit Brunn-Minkowski behavior. This
framework is further extended to accommodate different metrics and norms through the
introduction of a p-norm submodular measure. By leveraging this extension, we derive
a novel inequality for p-norm convex sets that generalizes the 1/2 and 2-norm Minkowski
inequalities. Finally, we provide an example illustrating the applicability of our
results to information-theoretic problems involving convex sets. This is achieved by
introducing a p-norm analog of the volume of a shadow, which is shown to be submodular.

This paper introduces an efficient solution to the 3D motion estimation problem using viewing graphs, which can be computed in O(n^3) time. The proposed method simplifies the process of finding a minimal spanning viewing graph through an iterative approach, starting with an initial graph and iteratively refining it until convergence. The process involves selecting a new node and updating the graph, which can be achieved in O(n^2) time per iteration. The proposed method significantly outperforms existing algorithms, achieving a speedup of one order of magnitude, and demonstrates its potential through applications in 3D reconstruction and image segmentation. Instead, we find that health insurance has a direct impact on the frequency of routine exams and overall health. Our results are consistent across different types of data and statistical analysis methods, and we also explore the potential for routine exams to explain the observed connection between health insurance and health outcomes. The interplay between turbulent friction and shock waves has a profound impact on shallow water flows, making it essential to accurately model these factors in simulations. By leveraging the water's energy dissipation and the Rankine-Hugoniot conditions, we develop a method to update the flow's properties, including water level and velocity, at each time step. This new scheme combines an energy-based formulation of the Darcy friction law with a shock-tracking method, enabling it to adapt friction coefficients and identify shock waves in real-time. Our approach is validated through numerical experiments in both subcritical and supersonic regimes, demonstrating its ability to converge to the exact solutions. Additionally, we compare our method with existing friction-colour schemes and show that it performs similarly, while offering a more robust and efficient framework for simulating shallow water flows. This new scheme is further applied to a two-dimensional dam-break test case, demonstrating its ability to accurately capture the complex dynamics of shallow water flows. This research aims to provide a comprehensive and efficient framework for simulating shallow water flows, with potential applications in various engineering fields. A novel method for evaluating the predictive performance of regression models has been developed by leveraging the variance of unseen data points. This approach, based on cross-validation tests, assesses the difference in variances between observed and unobserved data to determine a model's effectiveness. We demonstrate the theoretical soundness of this method through a proof of its asymptotic convergence in several commonly used loss functions. Furthermore, an empirical comparison of the proposed approach with traditional cross-validation methods through a series of experiments reveals that it can provide comparable or even better results. This new method is found to be particularly useful in scenarios where cross-validation tests fail to accurately identify the best-performing model. Our study also includes a case analysis of the impact of model characteristics on the proposed approach. In optimization theory, the implicit function theorem (IFT) is a foundational principle with far-reaching implications. Researchers have leveraged it to derive computational methods for determining gradients and Hessians in complex optimization problems, as well as establishing necessary conditions for optimization. This study delves into the algebraic properties of IFT, particularly its connections to commutative algebra and category theory. By examining these relationships, we seek to enhance our understanding of the theorem's underlying structure and its applications. The authors also investigate the potential of category theory in clarifying the relationships between different computational approaches to IFT. The ultimate goal of this research is to provide a comprehensive framework for comparing and evaluating computational methods for IFT. The study also touches on the potential for generalizing IFT through the concept of generalized implicit functions. Mathematical errors in models can result in physically inaccurate representations, with numerous instances documented across various scientific fields. To address this issue, researchers have developed advanced tools for identifying inconsistencies in step-by-step derivations. These methods are particularly useful for automating the verification of derivations created by humans. Our research focuses on the application of a newly introduced tool, called Proofreader, which utilizes a deep learning-based approach to assess the validity of mathematical derivations. In a comparative evaluation of Proofreader against existing state-of-the-art methods, our results reveal that it surpasses its rivals in detecting derivation flaws. To further demonstrate its capabilities, we apply Proofreader to a comprehensive collection of 1,500 derivations from 2019 Euro-Parallel Workshop on Machine Learning, and successfully identify 100 previously undetected errors. Our study demonstrates the potential of Proofreader to facilitate the creation of reliable, real-world models. Additionally, we release the tool's source code under an open-source license, making it available to the scientific community. Furthermore, we release a dataset comprising 1,500 manually verified mathematical derivations, accompanied by their corresponding ground truth, for the purpose of evaluating derivation verification tools. We introduce a pioneering human motion capture system that integrates data from IMUs and LiDAR sensors to provide precise long-term tracking even under varying sensor positions and environments. Our approach leverages a unique combination of deep learning techniques and Kalman filter updates to accurately track human movements over an extended period and on multiple days. Our results demonstrate that fusion of data from both IMUs and LiDAR significantly enhances accuracy compared to relying on a single sensor source. Additionally, we demonstrate that our system maintains consistent accuracy even when the sensor is moved, and that it can be successfully applied to real-world environments with diverse indoor and outdoor settings. The system's long-term tracking capabilities also enable the generation of high-quality 3D models from sequential motion capture data. All the necessary code and data to replicate our findings are available online. A video showcasing the system's performance can be viewed on YouTube. A novel approach to solving the crossing symmetry equations in the context of the conformal bootstrap problem involves harmonic analysis on the superconformal group $SU(N|3)$, a method that has been previously applied to $SU(N|1)$ with successful outcomes. The proposed method is expected to yield comparable results for the $N=4$ super-Yang-Mills theory, potentially leading to more precise upper bounds on the conformal bootstrap bounds. Furthermore, this approach is anticipated to be advantageous in the analysis of theories characterized by larger superconformal groups, thereby facilitating the cross-validation of the bootstrap predictions against field theory calculations. The current limitations of this method primarily stem from the challenges of accurately representing the $Y$-operators within the harmonic expansion. Nevertheless, a promising strategy for addressing this issue has been identified, involving the utilization of the conformal partial wave expansion.
